source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench: scientific equation discovery with LLMs
finding: Famous equations (Feynman set) look solved because models have memorised them. Rewriting them into less common forms (LSR-Transform) or inventing new terms (LSR-Synth) collapses accuracy.
numbers: 239 problems, 4 domains. Best system reached only 31.5% symbolic accuracy (LLM-SR with GPT-4o-mini, LSR-Transform). Same method on LSR-Synth with GPT-4o-mini: chemistry 11.1%, biology 16.7%, physics 9.9%, material science 20.2%. Direct prompting without data: 7.2% on LSR-Transform.
quote: best-performing system so far achieves only 31.5% symbolic accuracy
limits: Symbolic accuracy judged by an LLM against the target equation; only small open and mini models used as backbones.
agent_relevance: Rediscovery tests on textbook cases overstate ability. Evidence from historical cases must be checked against memorisation (use disguised or counterfactual versions).

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench: scientific equation discovery with LLMs
finding: Giving the model only the problem text (no data) is far worse than a loop that fits candidate equations to data and feeds the error back.
numbers: LSR-Transform symbolic accuracy: direct prompting 2-7%; LaSR 5-13% symbolic but 46-50% numeric Acc0.1; LLM-SR 11-31% symbolic. On LSR-Synth materials, LLM-SR numeric Acc0.1 82-88%.
limits: Different methods win on symbolic versus numeric metrics; GPT-3.5 backbone often worse than Llama-3.1-8B.
agent_relevance: Knowledge alone does not discover. The propose, fit, feed-back-the-residual loop is what moves results; it is the BACON-style data-driven cycle.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench: scientific equation discovery with LLMs
finding: Symbolic accuracy tracks out-of-domain extrapolation: right form means the law generalises.
numbers: All methods have higher NMSE out-of-domain than in-domain; the gap is larger for chemistry and biology than for physics and materials. Symbolic accuracy correlates positively with OOD Acc0.1.
limits: OOD sets exist only for the synthetic LSR-Synth problems.
agent_relevance: Add a held-out or extrapolation check before the agent declares a law found.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) NewtonBench: generalizable scientific law discovery in LLM agents
finding: 324 tasks over 12 physics domains built by counterfactual law shifts (altered known laws so memory does not help). Agents must probe a simulated system. Frontier reasoning models succeed in simple systems and fall off steeply in complex ones.
numbers: 11 LLMs, 4 runs each. Overall symbolic accuracy: GPT-5 75.9%, Gemini-2.5-pro 65.4%, GPT-5-mini 53.1%, o4-mini 47.8%, DeepSeek-R1 43.4%, Qwen3-235B 30.9%, GPT-4.1 5.8%, GPT-4.1-mini 5.1%. Hardest setting: GPT-5 40.3%, Gemini-2.5-pro 16.7%, all others below 6%.
quote: clear but fragile capability for discovery in frontier models
limits: Simulated physics; automatic symbolic equivalence; four runs per cell.
agent_relevance: Long deliberate reasoning matters far more than prompt style: all non-thinking models stay below 10% overall.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) NewtonBench: generalizable scientific law discovery in LLM agents
finding: A code interpreter helps weak models and slightly hurts strong ones. Strong models stop exploring early and settle for a decent fit.
numbers: Weak: GPT-4.1 5.8% to 18.9%, GPT-4.1-mini 5.1% to 14.7%. Strong: GPT-5 75.9% to 73.3%, Gemini-2.5-flash 50.6% to 40.9%, GPT-5-mini 53.1% to 48.1%. Exploration-token rate of Gemini-2.5-flash dropped sharply when code budget went from 0 to 1.
quote: premature shift from exploration to exploitation
limits: Exploration rate measured by keyword tokens (What if, Alternatively vs Confirm, Verify) in two models with visible traces; the mechanism is a hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence of premature exploitation. The schema should force a step that keeps rival hypotheses alive after the first good fit.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) NewtonBench: generalizable scientific law discovery in LLM agents
finding: Symbolic accuracy is very fragile to measurement noise even when fit error barely changes.
numbers: GPT-5-mini: noise of 0.0001 already cut symbolic accuracy by 12-16% versus noise-free; it fell steadily up to noise 0.1 while RMSLE stayed stable. Code access did not change this.
limits: One model used for the noise sweep.
agent_relevance: A good-looking fit is not evidence of the right law. Ask for a structural check, not only low error.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld: virtual environment for automated scientific discovery agents
finding: 120 tasks (8 topics x 3 difficulties) needing hypotheses, experiments and conclusions. Eleven practising scientists did the tasks; baseline agents did far worse, especially at explaining.
numbers: Humans (N=11, 1 hour limit): mean task completion 66%, knowledge discovered 55%, 11 of 16 tasks above 60%. Best agent REACT completed 38% of easy and 18% of challenge tasks. Best at knowledge (HYPOTHESIZER): 34% of gold knowledge on easy, 8% on challenge.
limits: Agents zero-shot with 2024 models; humans saw only normal and challenge levels, one seed.
agent_relevance: Agents managed unit-test sub-skills (60%+) but not the chain. The gap is in sequencing, which is what operator-sequence case studies describe.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld: virtual environment for automated scientific discovery agents
finding: Scoring has three parts: task completion, procedural steps, explanatory knowledge. A task can be finished without discovering the law.
numbers: Humans: knowledge score (55%) below completion (66%) because brute force solved tasks without the explanation.
limits: Knowledge scored by an LLM grader against a scorecard.
agent_relevance: Evaluate the agent on 'found the reason', not only 'got the answer'.

source: Yang et al. (2025) MOOSE-Chem: LLMs for rediscovering unseen chemistry hypotheses
finding: Hypothesis = background + inspirations. Retrieving the true inspiration paper from a corpus works surprisingly well even though it is an out-of-distribution step.
numbers: 51 chemistry papers from 2024 or later, GPT-4o cutoff before 2024. Hit ratio keeping top 4% of 300 papers: GPT-4o 83.7%, Llama-3.1-70B 83.0%, Llama-3.1-405B 78.7%, Llama-3.1-8B 43.5%. Corpus 1000: 88.9% at top 4%.
limits: Candidates are drawn around each paper's reference list; ground-truth inspirations are one reading of each paper.
agent_relevance: A worked model of a discovery case: background plus a distant source idea. Suggests an operator 'search a far domain for a bridging idea'.

source: Yang et al. (2025) MOOSE-Chem: LLMs for rediscovering unseen chemistry hypotheses
finding: Staged framework (multi-step inspiration, mutation, ranking) beats earlier hypothesis generators on matching real hypotheses.
numbers: GPT-4o-judged Top Matched Score: MOOSE-Chem 4.020, MOOSE 2.882, Qi et al. 2.686, SciMON 2.549. Without multi-step 3.765; without multi-step and evolutionary unit 2.863. Expert top-score counts over 51 cases: score 5: 0, 4: 2, 3: 19, 2: 16, 1: 8, 0: 6.
limits: Average Matched Score barely moves (2.56 vs 2.46 for MOOSE); the gain is in best-of-many. LLM judge in main table.
agent_relevance: Best-of-many generation plus ranking lifts the top result, not the average.

source: Liu et al. (2026) ResearchBench: LLMs in scientific discovery via inspiration-based task decomposition
finding: Benchmark over 12 disciplines using 2024+ papers to avoid contamination. Models are good at inspiration retrieval, weaker at ranking hypotheses.
numbers: Top-20% round: most models find about 80% of ground-truth inspirations (Llama-3.2-1B far lower). Final round (top 4%, 3 of 75 papers): above 40%, GPT-4o 45.65%. Extraction accuracy checked by 5 PhD students: 91.9% (major issues only), 82.3% (all issues).
limits: Extraction done by an LLM; table layout in the PDF text was garbled so some per-model figures were not verified.
agent_relevance: Ranking candidate ideas is a weak step. Do not let the model pick its own best hypothesis without an outside check.

source: Liu et al. (2026) ResearchBench: LLMs in scientific discovery via inspiration-based task decomposition
finding: In pairwise hypothesis ranking models show strong position bias (prefer the first option).
numbers: Error analysis text: 56% of errors judged as relevance misses (details of other categories 23%, 4% not fully verified).
limits: Percent breakdown read from a garbled PDF layout.
agent_relevance: Randomise order when the agent compares hypotheses.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Towards an AI co-scientist
finding: Multi-agent system with generation, debate (self-play), tournament ranking, evolution and meta-review. In a blind test it proposed the mechanism that a lab had found but not yet published.
numbers: Task: how capsid-forming phage-inducible chromosomal islands (cf-PICIs) spread across bacterial species. With minimal background it ranked first the hypothesis that they interact with diverse phage tails to widen host range. System took about 2 days.
limits: Single case, reported by the authors with the collaborating lab; public data may leak.
agent_relevance: Tournament plus evolution is a concrete hypothesis-refinement loop.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Towards an AI co-scientist
finding: Ablation on a 200-item rediscovery benchmark built from post-cutoff bioRxiv papers: outside search separates 'new' from 'already known'.
numbers: With search, novelty score for already-published ideas moved from 6.14 (wrongly novel) to 2.38 (correctly non-novel); correctness score 7.4 to 8.46. Different generation strategies were best on different tasks.
limits: Scores are LLM-given ratings; summary table partly garbled.
agent_relevance: Check novelty against the literature; self-judged novelty is inflated.

source: Mitchener et al. (2025) Kosmos: an AI scientist for autonomous discovery
finding: A shared structured world model keeps an agent coherent over about 200 rollouts and 12 hours. Three of seven highlighted discoveries reproduced unpublished or preprint work not seen at run time.
numbers: Average run: 42,000 lines of code, 1,500 papers read, 166 data-analysis and 36 literature rollouts. 79.4% of statements accurate (102 statements, 3 reports): 85.5% data analysis, 82.1% literature, 57.9% interpretation. Collaborators: a 20-cycle run is about 6 months of their work.
limits: Rated by collaborators; only 3 reports sampled; value claims self-reported.
agent_relevance: The weak point is interpretation (about 58%), the step case studies show is hardest. Keep a world model of what is known and tried.

source: Shojaee et al. (2024) LLM-SR: scientific equation discovery via programming with LLMs
finding: Equations as program skeletons proposed by the LLM from the scientific context, constants fitted by an optimiser, best kept in a multi-island memory.
numbers: Beat PySR and uDSR with 2.5K iterations versus 2M+. E. coli growth OOD NMSE 0.0037 vs above 1 for baselines. Ablation on Oscillation 2 (GPT-3.5): w/o iterative refinement NMSE 1.01e-1 ID and 1.81e-1 OOD; w/o skeleton+optimizer 3.78e-1 ID and 3.75e-1 OOD; w/o prior text and w/o program form also worse.
limits: Four author-built problems; LLM-SRBench later showed that much strength on classic forms may be recall.
agent_relevance: Stating the setting and variables in words is a useful step. An optimiser step separates structure from constants.

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench: data-driven discovery with LLMs
finding: 264 real tasks from papers plus 903 synthetic ones. The best agent scores about 25%. Reasoning scaffolds (ReAct, planner plus critic) did not beat a plain code-writing agent; oracle feedback did help.
numbers: Best performance about 25% hypothesis matching score. Reflexion with oracle HMS feedback over up to 3 trials improved over CodeGen; ReAct and DataVoyager did not. DB-REAL and DB-SYNTH scores similar. No-data guessing baseline about 13-16%.
limits: Three base models; matching judged by GPT-4; the no-data baseline shows memory contributes.
agent_relevance: Self-critique without an outside signal did not help; outside feedback did. Matches schema section 4b on unstructured self-reflection.

source: Chen et al. (2025) ScienceAgentBench
finding: 102 tasks from 44 papers, each a Python program. Simple loops beat heavy agents on cost-benefit.
numbers: Best agent with 3 attempts: 32.4% alone, 34.3% with expert knowledge. o1-preview with self-debug 42.2% at over 10x cost. Claude-3.5-Sonnet with self-debug solved 10.8% more tasks than OpenHands CodeAct at 17x lower cost.
limits: Task is code reproduction of published analysis, not new discovery.
agent_relevance: Self-debug with real execution feedback is cheap and strong; elaborate agents are not.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist
finding: End-to-end loop: idea, novelty check by search, code via Aider, experiments, write-up, automated review. The review step approximates human reviewers.
numbers: GPT-4o reviewer: 70% accuracy; balanced accuracy 0.65 vs 0.66 for humans on ICLR 2022 OpenReview. Reflexion +2% and one-shot +2% improved the reviewer. Claude Sonnet 3.5 gave the best papers.
limits: Template-bound ML tasks. Authors list failures: wrong novelty claims, buggy code, a worsened result reported as improvement.
agent_relevance: A full loop is possible, but self-reported results need independent verification.

source: Ma et al. (2025) AI-Newton: concept-driven physical law discovery without prior knowledge
finding: A symbolic system with a base of concepts and laws and plausible reasoning: if a law holds in many experiments but fails in one, add a simple term. It rediscovered Newton's second law, energy conservation and gravitation from 46 simulated mechanics experiments.
numbers: About 90 concepts and 50 general laws per case on average; max 1200 trials; about 48 hours runtime. Concepts appear in order: mass before force; potential energies appear while extending kinetic-energy conservation to springs.
limits: Simulated data; hand-designed concept language; not an LLM loop.
agent_relevance: A machine version of anomaly repair: when a law fails, add a term and keep the older law as a base. Operator candidate.

source: Shi et al. (2026) The Weight of Teamwork
finding: Fixed-budget LLM teams doing symbolic regression: spreading calls over independent tries beats talking among agents.
numbers: Ten independent trajectories vs one: mean held-out Q +0.70 (95% CI 0.41 to 1.03), median gain 0.11, 86 wins, 11 losses, 3 ties (100 Qwen problems). Ring communication lowered Q by 0.33 vs Independent; Star and Complete unresolved. Changing the final selection rule changed team rankings, even the sign for Complete.
limits: Exploratory; Qwen layer 100 problems, Terra layer 41; call budget and trajectory length change together.
agent_relevance: Independent attempts plus a good selection rule beat chatty teams. Report generation and selection separately.

source: Langley, Simon, Bradshaw, Zytkow (1987) Scientific Discovery: Computational Explorations of the Creative Process
finding: Production-system programs (BACON versions, GLAUBER, STAHL, DALTON, KEKADA and others) that rediscovered historical laws and theories from data using a few heuristics. Not opened this session; description from background knowledge.
numbers: Not checked this session.
limits: Rediscovery used data prepared by the authors; critics argued the representation did most of the work.
agent_relevance: Origin of the idea that a few general heuristics (find constants, find trends, introduce a new term as ratio or product) reproduce historical steps; LLM-SRBench and AI-Newton revive it.

source: Nickles (ed.) (1980) Scientific Discovery: Case Studies
finding: Edited volume of single-discovery histories. Not opened this session; no numbers claimed.
numbers: None.
limits: Case studies are retrospective narratives and can impose a neat order on a messy process.
agent_relevance: Source for operator sequences, but reconstructions come after the fact; test them with counterfactual cases (NewtonBench style).

source: Kulkarni and Simon (1988) The processes of scientific discovery: the strategy of experimentation (KEKADA)
finding: A program modelled on Hans Krebs's work on the urea cycle, with strategies such as look for surprise and follow the anomaly. Not opened this session.
numbers: None checked.
limits: One case.
agent_relevance: Template for an anomaly-driven loop: expect, observe, flag surprise, shift focus. Compare with NewtonBench premature exploitation.

source: Schmidt and Lipson (2009) Distilling free-form natural laws from experimental data
finding: Genetic search for equations recovered conservation laws from motion data. Cited by LLM-SRBench; not opened.
numbers: None checked.
limits: Evolutionary; no language model.
agent_relevance: Baseline family that LLM-SR and LaSR compete against.
